name: merge for counters
desc: Adds a value to the number stored under a key, inserting it when the key is new. One call replaces the get, null check, and put sequence.

name: compute and computeIfPresent
desc: Rebuilds the value for a key from the old value. Returning null removes the entry, which makes conditional updates a single call.
body:
`computeIfAbsent` is the one to reach for when grouping: it only runs the lambda on a miss, so the list is created once and then reused. `computeIfPresent` skips missing keys entirely. `compute` always runs and receives null for a miss.

Do not modify the same map from inside the lambda. The update is already in progress, and a nested put on the same key is undefined behaviour for most implementations.

name: floorKey and ceilingKey
desc: Returns the nearest key at or below, or at or above, the given key. Both return null when no such key exists.
body:
The four methods come in key and entry pairs: `floorKey`, `floorEntry`, `ceilingKey`, `ceilingEntry`. Strict neighbours are `lowerKey` and `higherKey`, which exclude an exact match.

`firstKey` and `lastKey` read the ends. All of them are logarithmic, so a price band lookup stays cheap on a large table.

name: subMap range view
desc: Returns a view of the entries between two keys. The booleans decide whether each bound is included.
body:
`headMap(to, inclusive)` and `tailMap(from, inclusive)` are the one sided forms. Without the boolean, `subMap(from, to)` includes the low key and excludes the high one.

A view is not a copy. Removing through it changes the original map, and adding a key outside the range throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Copy into an `ArrayList` when the caller needs an independent snapshot.

name: TreeSet with a tie breaker
desc: Keeps elements sorted and unique by the comparator. A comparator that ignores a field treats two different rows as the same element.
body:
Inside a `TreeSet`, `compare` returning 0 means duplicate, whatever `equals` says. The set never calls `equals`.

This bites in reports sorted by one field: the set looks correct, the count is short. Add every field that identifies a row, or use a `HashSet` when order does not matter.

name: retainAll and removeAll
desc: Keeps only the elements also present in another collection, or drops every element found there. Both edit the set in place.
body:
`retainAll` returns true when the set changed, so it doubles as a change check.

Copy first when the original set must survive. `removeAll` on the original is the common slip: the report then runs on an emptied set. For a union, add everything into a copy instead.

Both methods are linear in the smaller collection's size when the argument is a set.

name: ListIterator insert and set
desc: Edits a list at the cursor while walking it. add inserts before the cursor, set replaces the last element returned by next.
body:
`list.listIterator(size)` starts at the end, so `hasPrevious` and `previous` walk backwards. That is the only cheap reverse walk on a list.

The same work with `list.add` inside a for-each loop throws `ConcurrentModificationException`, because the list changes outside the loop's own cursor. Removal through `it.remove()` is legal for the same reason.

name: Deque as a stack
desc: push and pop act on the front of the deque, which gives LIFO behaviour without the legacy Stack class.
body:
`pop` on an empty deque throws `NoSuchElementException`, while `peek` returns null. Check `isEmpty` when the stack can run dry.

`ArrayDeque` rejects null elements, so a null answer from `peek` can only mean empty. The front is also the queue head: `offerLast` and `pollFirst` make the same object a FIFO queue.

name: PriorityQueue order
desc: Hands out the smallest element by comparator instead of the oldest. It implements Queue but is not first in, first out.
body:
The heap only guarantees the head. Iterating or printing the queue shows the internal array order, not sorted order, so drain it with `poll` when the order matters.

`add` and `offer` are both logarithmic. Equal keys are ordered arbitrarily, so add a tie breaker when the output must be reproducible.

name: LRU cache with LinkedHashMap
desc: Keeps the most recently used entries up to a limit and drops the least recently used one. Access order plus one overridden method is the whole cache.
body:
The third constructor argument is the switch: `true` tracks access order, `false` tracks insertion order. `removeEldestEntry` runs after every put and returns true to delete the head of the order.

The class is not thread safe. Wrap it in `Collections.synchronizedMap` only when every compound operation is also guarded, because a get followed by a put is two steps.

name: equals and hashCode for a key
syntax: equals(Object) and hashCode() over the same fields
desc: A key class must return equal hash codes for equal objects, or map and set lookups miss. A record generates both methods.
body:
`Objects.hash` boxes its arguments, so a class hashed in a tight loop can use `31 * a + b` by hand instead. Correctness does not change.

Never change a field used by `hashCode` after the object enters a map or set. The entry stays in the old bucket and both `get` and `contains` stop finding it. `record` fields are final, which removes the risk.

name: Collections.frequency
desc: Counts how many elements equal the given value. Linear in the collection size, so it is fine for one value and wrong inside a loop over many values.
body:
`frequency` uses `equals`, so it works on records and strings without extra code. A custom class needs `equals` for the comparison to mean anything.

A loop of `frequency` calls is quadratic: every call walks the whole list. The single map pass is linear and gives every count at once.
